 If I keep these 22 sites the uncertainty in the occupancy and detection parameters will increase and preclude my comparison of occupancy between ERAs?

Thanks

Best

We have been capturing/resighting sparrows during three winter capture windows to get winter survival with Cormack-Jolly-Seber models. The capture windows are usually 1-2 weeks so we can accommodate multiple sites from North Carolina to Delaware. All of the resights/recaptures that we have had until now were at the site that they were originally banded. However, last week we captured a bird in Virginia and then recaptured the same bird at a different site a few days later in Delaware.

I am not sure exactly how to handle this bird as we are using latitude and a site-specific vegetation index as covariates. Can anyone point me to a paper where something like this happened? I think it is unusual but this cant be the first time a bird has flown from one study site to the next in a short period of time.

Hi Chris,

You can compute model-averaged predictions in ‘unmarked’ (as you did in your code), but you can’t average coefficients. If you want to do the latter, you could use the ‘AICCmodavg’ package. Just be aware of the pitfalls of averaging coefficients, some of which are described in this paper: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/14-1639.1.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Model averaging in pcountOpen
messages.body_plain:
Hi Leo,

Here are some suggestions:

1) You should not skim down the candidate model set when it comes to
compute model-averaged coefficients or predictions - you should be
using the entire set of models. You risk overestimating the effect of
certain parameters. Use all your models.

2) Instead of trying to average coefficients from each parameter, you
should be working on averaging predictions for some values of your
explanatory variables that are of interest to you. For example, if you
want to get predictions of abundance at different seasons, use each
model to make a prediction for lambda and then model-average those
predictions. If you want latent values (e.g., from ranef( )), you can
extract them from each model, and then model-average these values if
you want. You will have to use a couple of loops, but is not that
difficult to do.

3) If you want to present predictions in a plot, you need to vary only
one variable and keep the others constant. Otherwise, you will get
nonsensical lines or points. For example, if you want to show the
effect of crop on abundance, vary crop and keep all other variables
constant:

pred_data1<-data.frame(crop=seq(min(est_500$crop),
                       max(est_500$crop),length.out = 30),
                       grass=mean(est_500$grass))

Then, you can model-average the predictions.

Good luck,

Marc

You have at least one site (AP_E09) that has 3 observations:

table(inp$Point_ID)

Perhaps that is a mistake in the raw data, if you change it to the correct Point_ID and run formatLong, you should end up with only two observations.

You can use
siteCovs(fl)

and
obsCovs(fl)

to look and check if it looks like they have been read in right. To be honest I would advise against using csvToUMF or formatLong, and rather read the documentation for unmarkedFrameOccu() carefully and build the frame manually yourself to make sure it's exactly how you want it.

You're correct that your counts are being truncated to 0/1 every time you run a occu model. There are similar types of models for count data, e.g. N-mixture models which can be fit with the pcount() function in unmarked. There are advantages and disadvantages to this vs. occupancy models that depend on your research questions, experimental design, and dataset. I would suggest you look at the relevant chapters of one of the available textbooks, e.g. Marc & Andy's "Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology" to help you decide which fits your situation best.

Ken

There are a number of resources out there to get better acquainted with these methods (including the original papers).

A common approach is to use the mean values of the predictor variables to get a point estimate for occupancy and detection probability. If your predictor variables are scaled (so that they have a mean of 0 and a st. deviation of 1), then getting the point estimates at predictor values of 0 probably makes sense. If you did not scale the predictor variables, then getting the point estimates of occupancy and detection probability at predictor values of 0 probably does not make sense (e.g. what would it mean to have a DBH of 0?). You could get the point estimates at the mean predictor values by doing something like:
> backTransform(linearComb(fm4, coefficients = c(1, mean(data$CAMHEIGHT)), type = 'det'))

Philip Shirk

messages.body_plain:
A few thoughts:
Option 1: use open-population models (see here <https://sci-hub.se/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2010.01465.x> and here <https://sci-hub.se/10.1890/14-1487.1>). These are implemented in unmarked via the pcountOpen <https://rdrr.io/cran/unmarked/man/pcountOpen.html> function.
Option 2: use models that do not require replicate sampling (see here <https://sci-hub.se/10.1002/env.1149>). You can fit these models in the 'detect <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/detect/index.html>' R package using the svabu <https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/detect/versions/0.4-2/topics/svabu> and svocc  <https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/detect/versions/0.4-2/topics/svocc>functions
Note that these models can be very sensitive to model assumptions and so might give very biased estimates (see here <https://sci-hub.se/10.1111/2041-210X.12329> and here <https://sci-hub.se/10.1111/2041-210X.12432>).
Option 3: use Poisson regression models that do not explicitly estimate absolute abundance (see here <https://sci-hub.se/10.1111/biom.12734>). You could still model variation in detectability and abundance through space or time, you just won't get estimates of absolute abundance.
Option 4: use all 3 of the above methods and see if they give similar results. If they do, great! If they don't, you'll need to think more about why some of the models are biased/inaccurate.
Philip Shirk

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Back Transforming for 'det'
messages.body_plain:
For models with a single observational covariate rather than selecting just one predicted detection probability, I would say you want to look at all of them (with "all of them" meaning across the complete range of the values of the observational covariate).  Including confidence bands would also be warranted:  "A statistic is at best of unknown value without a measure of precision."  Here's a brute force example using data included with unmarked:

> # Get data
>   library(unmarked)
>   pcru <- csvToUMF(system.file("csv","frog2001pcru.csv", package="unmarked"),
>     long = TRUE, type = "unmarkedFrameOccu")
>
> # Run occu
>   fm <- occu(~Temperature ~ 1, pcru, control=list(reltol=1e-12))
>
> # Make predictions over the range of observed temperatures
>   tempMin <- min(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
>   tempMax <- max(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
>   temp <- tempMin + (tempMax-tempMin)*c(0:100)/100
>   prob <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[2]+fm@opt$par[3]*temp))
>
> # Plot estimated detection curve
>   plot(temp, prob, type="l", xlab="Temperature (degrees C)",
>     ylab="Detection probability", cex.lab=1.5, font.lab=2, las=1,
>     ylim=c(0,1), lwd=3)
>
> # Add in approximate 95% confidence band
>   v <- vcov(fm)
>   se <- (v[2,2] + temp^2 * v[3,3] + 2*temp*v[2,3])^0.5
>   lines(temp,  1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[2]+fm@opt$par[3]*temp + 1.96*se)), lty=3)
>   lines(temp,  1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[2]+fm@opt$par[3]*temp - 1.96*se)), lty=3)
>
>
>
> When there are two observational covariates one could construct a contour plot:
>
> > # Get data
> >   library(unmarked)
> >   pcru <- csvToUMF(system.file("csv","frog2001pcru.csv", package="unmarked"),
> >     long = TRUE, type = "unmarkedFrameOccu")
> >
> > # Run occu
> >   fm2 <- occu(~ MinAfterSunset + Temperature ~ 1, pcru)
> >
> > # Construct contour plot on a 101 x 101 array over the observed
> > # range of observational covariates.
> >   masMin <- min(pcru@obsCovs$MinAfterSunset, na.rm=TRUE)
> >   masMax <- max(pcru@obsCovs$MinAfterSunset, na.rm=TRUE)
> >   tempMin <- min(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
> >   tempMax <- max(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
> >   prob <- matrix(rep(NA,101^2), nrow=101)
> >   mas <- masMin + (masMax-masMin)*c(0:100)/100
> >   temp <- tempMin + (tempMax-tempMin)*c(0:100)/100
> >   for (i in 1:101) {
> >   for (j in 1:101) {
> >       prob[i,j] = 1 - 1/(1+exp(sum(fm2@opt$par[2:4]*c(1, mas[i], temp[j]))))
> >   }}
> >   contour(mas, temp, prob, xlab="Time after sunset (min)",
> >     ylab="Temperature (degrees C)", main="Detection probabilities",
> >     cex.lab=1.5, font.lab=2, cex.main=2, las=1, labcex=1)
> >
> >
> >
> > And if you're as extreme as I am, one could also create a spinning 3D plot with the predicted detection probability surface sandwiched by the lower and upper confidence surfaces.
> >
> > Jim
> >

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mike,
I'm not super familiar with the eDNAoccupancy package, but believe that it might only allow for single season estimation.

There is a multiseason implementation of the multi-method model. It is developed here: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ece3.4822, and the authors include JAGS code. This multiseason version is also available in Program MARK.

The mutliseason model comes at a cost of estimating additional parameters. Your sample size of 12 sites is on the small size, so it might be better to run two single season models and to make comparisons between them.

Best,
Brittany
